description.value: Followers of Azal who separated from Baháʼuʼlláh following his public declaration in Edirne, remaining technically Bábís and retaining a stance of militancy and political activism. Following accusations of sedition lodged by the Azalís against Baháʼuʼlláh, the Ottoman government investigated and ultimately banished Baháʼuʼlláh to Acre and Azal to Cyprus.

The definitive schism between the Azalís and Baháʼís occurred in Adrianople (Edirne) between 1866 and 1868. While most Bábís accepted Baháʼuʼlláh's claim to be 'Him whom God shall make manifest' and became Baháʼís, the minority remaining loyal to Azal and the Bayán were referred to as Azalís or Azalí Bábís.

Regarded as heretics for believing in a post-Muḥammadan revelation, Baháʼís continued to suffer severe discrimination, mob violence, and killings in Iran—where several hundred more were slain prior to 1925—as well as harsh treatment by the Sunni Ottoman authorities. This persistent persecution acted as a major catalyst driving Baháʼís to flee Iran and establish communities in Russian-administered territories such as Transcaspia and the Caucasus.

description.value: Valentin Alekseevich Zhukovskii was a Russian Orientalist specializing in Persian language and dialects, literature, folklore, history, and ethnography. He served as a professor at St Petersburg University (1886–1918), dean of the Faculty of Oriental Languages (1902–1911), and director of the Educational Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (1905–1917), and was a corresponding member of the Russian Academy of Sciences from 1899.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 1, p. 205–206 (biographical note)

draft_notes: Years of birth and death are 1858–1918 (exact dates 6 May [O.S. 24 April] 1858 – 17 January 1918 unverified from general knowledge). A student and close friend of Baron Viktor Rozen, he also collected documents and information regarding Bábís and Baháʼís during his travels in Iran and Transcaspia.

description.value: Nikolai Karlovich Girs (Nicholas de Giers) was a Russian diplomat of Scandinavian Protestant ancestry who worked in the Asian Department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs from 1838 and was appointed first secretary in Istanbul in 1850. He served as minister in Ṭihrán from 1863, director of the Asian Department and deputy minister of foreign affairs from 1875, and minister of foreign affairs from 1882.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 2, p. 172 (biographical note)

draft_notes: The biographical note gives only the years of birth and death (1820–1895), not exact dates in YYYY-MM-DD format. Exact dates from general knowledge (unverified): born 21 May 1820 (9 May O.S.) near Radziwiłłów, Volhynian Governorate, Russian Empire; died 26 January 1895 (14 January O.S.) in St. Petersburg, Russian Empire.

description.value: Matvei Avel’evich Gamazov was a Russian diplomat, translator, teacher of Turkish in the Educational Department of Oriental Languages of the Asian Department of the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and head of the department from 1872 to 1893. He was Aleksandr Tumanskii’s teacher and interested him in the study of Bábism.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 1, p. 194 (biographical note); vol. 2, p. 172 (biographical note); vol. 1, p. 65

draft_notes: Sources specify birth year 1812 and death year 1893, but do not provide full YYYY-MM-DD dates. Vol. 2, p. 66 also notes his civil rank as Privy Counsellor.

description.value: In Russian accounts in Transcaspia, local Christians viewed the Bábís with high sympathy, placing them, relative to morality, immensely higher than Persians who did not adhere to their teaching. The religion's texts were characterized as having a moral-religious content and forming a high moral-social system that appeals to lofty ideals in daily life.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 2, p. 67; vol. 2, p. 92; vol. 2, p. 153

draft_notes: This entry reflects the topical index subject 'morality' from Russian administrative and ethnographic reports assessing Bábí and Bahá'í ethics, social conduct, and communal reputation in Transcaspia.

description.value: French diplomat and author who held diplomatic posts in Europe from 1849 to 1854 before serving in Ṭihrán as first secretary of the French legation (1855), chargé d'affaires (1856–1858), and minister in Iran (1862–1863). His account of the Bábí movement in Les religions et les philosophies dans l'Asie centrale was widely influential.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 2, p. 172 (biographical note)

draft_notes: Sources provide lifedates only as years (1816–1882); exact YYYY-MM-DD values are not given in the text, so birth_date and death_date are set to null. Unverified facts from general knowledge: born 14 July 1816 in Ville-d'Avray, France; died 13 October 1882 in Turin, Italy. Sources also note his use of Sipihr's Násikh al-Taváríkh and his translation of the 'livre des préceptes' (Bayan).

description.value: Nikolai Vladimirovich Khanykov (1822–1878) was a Russian diplomat and Orientalist who served in the diplomatic department in the Caucasus and as head of the consulate-general in Tabríz. A corresponding member of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, he authored numerous scientific publications in history, geography, and ethnology, and collected Bábí manuscripts.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 1, p. 197–198 (biographical note)

draft_notes: Sources specify only the years of birth and death (1822–1878), not exact dates (YYYY-MM-DD). From general knowledge (unverified): Khanykov was born on 24 October 1822 in Kaluga Governorate, Russian Empire, and died on 15 November 1878 in Rambouillet, France. Russian name: Николай Владимирович Ханыков.

description.value: Vasilii Vladimirovich Bartol’d was a Russian Orientalist who specialized in the history of the Middle East, making his primary contribution in the medieval history of Central Asia and Iran. Born in St Petersburg to a Russianized German family, he studied under Viktor Rozen at St Petersburg University, where he taught from 1896 until the end of his life. Over his career, he published 670 works, including 247 articles in the Encyclopedia of Islam.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 1, p. 191 (biographical note)

draft_notes: The sources give only birth and death years (1869–1930); exact YYYY-MM-DD dates are unverified from external knowledge as 15 November 1869 – 19 August 1930. In Western scholarship he is frequently known as Wilhelm Barthold or Vasily Barthold. In 1924, he purchased the 'Hudud al-'Alam' ('Tumanskii's Manuscript') from Tumanskii's widow and transferred it to the Asiatic Museum / Institute of Oriental Studies, later publishing a facsimile edition in 1930.

description.value: Russian diplomat and author who served in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and in the Russian religious mission in China and Korea. He collected ethnographic information about Korea that formed the basis of his posthumously published book, Ocherki Korei (Sketches of Korea), and was heading the Russian diplomatic mission in Tehran as chargé d’affaires when he died at his post.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 2, p. 180 (biographical note)

draft_notes: The biographical note on vol. 2, p. 180 dates his life to 1850–1889 and states that he died at his post in Tehran as chargé d'affaires. However, documents dated 27 February 1890 and 10 September 1890 (vol. 2, pp. 56, 58) are attributed by the volume editors to 'Envoy [M. A. Podzhio]'.

description.value: Russian diplomat who served as secretary of the Russian legation in Madrid, the Hague, Naples, and Istanbul, and was minister in Ṭihrán (1846–1854) during the period of upheavals and persecutions connected to the spread of the Bábí movement and the execution of the Báb.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 1, p. 193 (biographical note)

draft_notes: Sources give birth and death years as (1797–1867), but specific calendar dates (YYYY-MM-DD) are not provided. There is a slight discrepancy in the sources regarding the start of his post in Ṭihrán: the biographical notes (vol. 1, p. 193; vol. 2, p. 171) give 1846–54, while text narratives (vol. 1, pp. 15, 52) give 1845–54. Unverified general knowledge: Russian form Князь Дмитрий Иванович Долгоруков; born 10 August 1797, died 19 October 1867.

description.value: A European power that engaged in the nineteenth-century regional rivalry with Russia known as the 'Great Game', containing Iran in southern Iraq, Afghanistan, and the Persian Gulf. In its efforts to strengthen its influence in Iran, it secured economic monopolies and supported politicians such as Ẓill al-Sulṭán, while refraining from intervening on behalf of the persecuted Bábís so as not to alienate the Persian clergy and population.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 1, p. 14

draft_notes: Coordinates not mentioned in the source; unverified coordinates for Great Britain are approximately 55.3781° N, 3.4360° W. In the nineteenth century, the sovereign state was formally the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.

variant_labels.value: Mirza Taqi Khan Farahani Amir Kabir

description.value: Mírzá Taqí Khán, Amír Kabír, served as prime minister of Iran under Náṣir al-Dín Sháh Qájár, influencing the monarch to begin introducing reforms. In 1850, he ordered the transfer and execution of the Báb, assigning the execution to his brother Mírzá Ḥasan Khán Vazír-i Niẓám.
description.source: Shahvar et al., The Baha'is of Iran, Transcaspia and the Caucasus, vol. 1, p. 15

draft_notes: The sources mention his death and the general discontent following it, but do not provide specific birth or death dates. From general knowledge (unverified): born Mírzá Muḥammad Taqí Khán Faráhání c. 1807 in Hazaveh near Arak; executed on 10 January 1852 in the Fin Garden bathhouse in Kashan.
